extracted.intended_audience: politically engaged readers of the Public Advertiser; 18th-century British electorate and commentators
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and reasoning in a politically persuasive pamphlet/letter addressing parliamentary law, precedent, and public opinion; focuses on interpretation of parliamentary votes and consequences for public rights. Meant to guide crafting legal-political argument and persuading a broad public readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual interpretation of parliamentary votes
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret the effect of a parliamentary resolution from the precise terms and grammatical structure of the vote (e.g., whether incapacity is attached to expulsion alone or to expulsion together with commitment to the Tower).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the vote literally and syntactically; avoid reading in unstated inferences. Example anti-pattern: assuming incapacity derives from expulsion alone when the vote's wording links multiple facts. If ambiguity exists, quote the resolution verbatim to show meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on historical precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Use prior cases and parliamentary practice (e.g., Mr. Wollaston's 1698 case) as authoritative guides to current questions of parliamentary law and eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite concrete historical examples to rebut novel assertions. Treat strong, clear precedents as 'land-marks' that constrain present actions. Beware of dismissing inconvenient precedents without addressing their facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid absurd legal constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject interpretations of law that lead to manifestly absurd consequences (for instance, treating commitment to the Tower as a constituent cause of legal incapacity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test proposed legal interpretations by their logical consequences. If an interpretation forces parties to accept an implausible premise, label it absurd and show a better construction. Use dialectical reasoning to expose absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish punishment from the underlying offense
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate whether incapacity is grounded on the criminal act (the offence) or on the subsequent punishment or sanction (the commitment/expulsion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue carefully whether the declaration of incapacity is tied to the fact of punishment or to the fact of guilt; support claim with text of the vote and precedents. Clarify that conflating punishment and offence creates legal confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity in recording grounds for legislative action
rubrics_metrics.description: When a legislative body intends to create incapacity or disability, it should state the crimes or grounds in the same resolution to avoid public confusion about the basis of the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If drafting or critiquing resolutions, insist that the body explicitly list the factual grounds if it intends those facts to be the source of disability. Anti-pattern: vague resolutions that mix punishment and alleged crimes, leaving electors uncertain of legal effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the central legal question, not case merits
rubrics_metrics.description: In argumentation, separate the interpretive/legal question (e.g., does expulsion create incapacity?) from the moral or factual merits of an individual's conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid being sidetracked by debating whether the person deserved punishment; concentrate on what the law or resolution actually does. State explicitly when you are limiting your enquiry to intent/meaning rather than justice of the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical/dialectical rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply clear dialectical logic and knowledge of argumentative principles to interpret votes and expose fallacies (e.g., use of syllogistic reasoning to show inconsistent conclusions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elementary rules of logic and plain English grammar to test constructions. Point out equivocations and misquotations. Anticipate counter-arguments and reduce them to contradiction where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess precedent for long-term constitutional effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate decisions not only for immediate effect but for the precedent they set and their consequences for future rights and parliamentary power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue about the broader political-constitutional implications of a ruling or vote; warn how a precedent may be 'dangerous' to posterity. Use hypothetical future scenarios to illustrate risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for exceptions and special statuses
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing cases, account for institutional or status-based exceptions (e.g., clergy have separate parliamentary privileges) that make precedents non-analogous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine factual distinctions between cases before claiming precedent. Identify status-based legal rules and confirm whether they alter applicability of earlier decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support public argument with primary texts and quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting an interpretation to the public, publish the actual resolution, votes, or other primary documents with solemnity to let readers judge the wording for themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide verbatim quotations of the contested text; where possible, reproduce the resolution exactly. This strengthens credibility and prevents charge of misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare authoritative sources to expose contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Test the ministry's assertions by comparing leading authorities (e.g., Dr. Blackstone) and highlight contradictions to undermine misplaced claims of unified legal support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote and juxtapose authoritative passages that conflict to show inconsistency. Use such contradictions to argue that the opposing position lacks coherent legal foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect individual/common rights against arbitrary parliamentary power
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue that subjects' common rights should not be extinguished by a mere capricious vote of one branch of the legislature; resist constructions that allow arbitrary deprivation of rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the issue in terms of fundamental rights and constitutional duty; appeal to history and ancestors to strengthen the normative case. Portray arbitrary power as illegitimate even if technically enacted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use moral and emotional appeals to mobilize public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoke duty to ancestors, obligation to posterity, personal conscience, and the shame of surrendering rights to rouse public sentiment and encourage civic action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance legal argument with moral exhortation: remind readers of inheritance of rights, the dishonor of surrendering them, and personal stakes. Example: contrast a life of freedom with mere existence to stir indignation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call out sophistry and falsehood explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Label evasive or inconsistent ministerial arguments as sophistry, falsehood, or impudence to delegitimize them rhetorically and logically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point to exact instances of evasion, shifting grounds, or invented distinctions. Use strong, precise language to characterize bad-faith arguments while backing claims with facts and quotations.
